subject: Critical Thinking
subcategory: Evidence & Truth: How We Know What's Real
title: Testimony and Trust: When to Believe Others
description: One-minute skill: Testimony and Trust: When to Believe Others.

hook.text: You believe the Earth orbits the Sun. Have you verified it yourself? No. You trust scientists.

buildup.text: Testimony – information from others – is our primary knowledge source.

discovery.text: Reliable testimony comes from credible sources, corroborated accounts, and consistent track records.

twist.text: But expertise in one field doesn't transfer. A Nobel physicist's opinion on economics deserves no special weight.

climax.text: The key question: does this person have both the expertise AND the incentive alignment to tell the truth?

punchline.text: Trust isn't binary. It's calibrated to track record and incentives.

quiz.question: What makes testimony reliable?
options: Credibility, corroboration, and consistent track records

details.summary: Testimony is evidence based on someone else's report. Most of what you know comes from testimony, not personal experience. Evaluating testimony requires judging the competence and honesty of the source.
details.whyItMatters: Since you cannot personally verify most claims, knowing how to evaluate testimony is essential for navigating information responsibly.
takeaways: Most human knowledge depends on trusting others' reports
Competence and honesty are the two pillars of credible testimony
Corroboration from independent sources increases reliability

faq.question: How can you evaluate whether someone's testimony is reliable?
faq.answer: Check their expertise in the relevant domain, look for potential biases or conflicts of interest, see if independent sources corroborate the claim, and consider whether they have a track record of accuracy.

faq.question: Why is independent corroboration so important for testimony?
faq.answer: A single witness can be mistaken, biased, or dishonest. When multiple independent sources report the same thing, the probability of all of them being wrong drops dramatically. Independence is the key — coordinated sources do not count.
